speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: Sure, that sounds great. I decided to run for the school board back October when I was on the way home from attending the hearing. It was an educational practices commission hearing for our superintendent in Manatee County Cynthia Saunders, who had been accused of and found guilty of over inflating graduation rates to try to manipulate the district grade and the school grades. The process by which she did this was micro-targeting a small group of students whose families were very disenfranchised, who many did not speak any English. Many were fearful of their immigration status. And suddenly these children were arriving at school or getting phone calls to their homes and saying you're no longer enrolled in public school. I'm in Manatee County any longer. And then when the state-- this was flagged by the state when they kept seeing all of these students who were being coded in Manatee County as homeschoolers because it was one thing to just leave these kids out the street. It was another thing you had to code them in a certain way. So she chose to make them all homeschoolers. She also did this with kids who genuinely were dropping out of high school in Manatee County. Some kids went on to get a GED. And if that were the case, those children were again not flagged as dropouts. They were flagged as being homeschooled. So when the state came in with investigators and did a full investigation, they couldn't find any paperwork. And that provided them with a parent signature that said this child was being homeschooled. And many parents were receiving angry phone calls from the state saying, where's your portfolio? Where's your work? Your homeschooling your child. And that was kind of the first they were hearing this. And because she chose such a very vulnerable population, that was never really brought to the attention of anybody in the public sphere. It was just kind of kept quiet for a long, long time until it wasn't the mistake got involved. So at that practices commission, we were able to see a couple of us all got on a bus to watch this. And the practices commission denied her the sediment that was negotiated on her behalf. That the taxpayers had paid tens of thousands of dollars to be for. And it was to try to allow her to save her teaching certificate and then her position as superintendent of Manatee County School. The school board knew all about this scandal. They knew it had been going on. And yet they still gave her the job. She was a deputy superintendent. They promoted her to full superintendent, even though they had all this information. The settlement was denied. And so it went back to the attorneys. And it all has to be negotiated on the taxpayer time again. So it's been very frustrating because the practices commission said, why did your district tire her? Why did they promote her if they knew this information? Why we would like to see her license suspended. That's what we are requesting happen. How much can come to us with some sort better settlement? So it's been a little frustrating. But that was kind of the day. As I wrote home on that bus, I thought, you know what? Just this is not being served here. And there are a lot of children who did not receive their right to a free and appropriate public education in Manatee County. And I really felt inclined to get involved and to do something more than just coming from the perspective of just being a citizen, where citizens were not being heard. We were being ignored, even though we had gone to multiple board meetings to say, we don't feel right about this superintendent. We don't feel comfortable. We want to do a national search. And we were just -- we just were not listened to. So that's kind of what got me on the bandwagon to run. And in the meantime, I was a teacher for a long time. I have a master's degree in education. And I was a Florida teacher for two years in Manatee. And then I taught in the city of Chicago in Title I schools in the south and the west sides. And I was also a teacher in New York for a short while, where I did get my master's degree. So that's kind of been my experience. And so when I realized that education was changing dramatically, not only in the county, but in the state as well, I decided to leave education. And it was really heartbreaking. And I do miss it every day. But sometimes I feel like I'm doing some better work on the outside. And I'm hoping to do even more-- make more changes, positive changes, especially for more vulnerable communities as an elected school board member.

transcript: . First, I would start off with, just in regard to the budget and finance, we spend a tremendous amount of our budgets-- our budget on administrative costs. And I didn't realize how egregious it was until I started really carefully going through school board agenda. I attend many school board meetings, and before I go, I always make sure to download the agenda. I look at what they're loading on. And her predecessor, Cynthia Sounder's predecessor, was very big on changing job descriptions and job titles. And kind of almost-- I don't want to say dumbing down the position, but taking out certain really important requirements that people needed at very high levels of the administration to be qualified for some of these jobs. For example, the head of HR did not have special HR certification or a background in HR. She had been a teacher. So I saw these odd promotions taking place. And it really affected hiring and payroll. And it had effects on the teachers because so many of these people at the top tier of these OCS administrations were just not qualified for some of the positions they were in. So we watched over the last couple of years as they continuously changed these job descriptions. And in the meantime, when Sounder's came on, she's actually created even more leadership positions. Her most recent was an assistant deputy superintendent of finance, business and finance. And so there was a job description that the board approved for this new position. The board approved all of it. And then they always give a salary guideline, like if whoever we hire, the salary is either $90,000 to $148,000. And with every single position that Sounder's has filled with these top tier, these people don't start off at $90,000 and give them something to work towards, or they always start out at the top end of a salary scale. And it is maddening to me. We've lost two CEOs, Manicani School CEOs. We lost two in one year. That's last year. So because of some catchy things that were done with money, and here we bring in this new person, and we have to elevate them to the level of the deputy superintendent instead of just CEO. And then we have to pay them at the tip of the top of the pay scale. So that's one of the things that I found very, very frustrating. And I wouldn't have known any of this unless I had taken some time to go through each and every agenda before the board meetings. That's a pet peeve of mine. It's very frustrating. What it is enabled a superintendent to do is have a level of loyalty with her inside people. And that allowed her to inflate graduation rates. This actually was seen in the inspector general's report, which was approximately 140 pages. It's an interesting read if anybody would like to see it. It's public record. And you can see where her top level people in that cabinet all knew this was going on. And they were putting pressure on people under them to change code and to push these kids out of school. And it's not OK. And a lot of them are certified or qualified to be in some of the positions that they're in. So issues like curriculum instruction arise or finance arise or things like that. Our new finance director, though, is the deputy superintendent was a longtime finance person in schools across the state of Florida. So I could comfortably have background in it. But what was the purpose of having Kevin come in at such a high level, that's such, you know, the end of the paper, top end of the pay scale? So that was one thing. And then the other thing I have great concerns with the start of finance is the amount of money that we spend on educational technology. I'm not anti-computer. I'm not anti-tech. But what I'm not OK with as an educator is millions and millions that we spend every year on products that are not properly researched, that are not peer reviewed, they're not third party reviewed. And we don't have the data to support to continually purchasing these products. We're not even seeing that within our district itself, test scores are, you know, going through the roof. I mean, if test scores were so great, our superintendent would not cook books to make us stay a B district, because that's pretty much what we are and what we've always been. And it's really kind of been by the skin of our teeth. So we have a group of students, our special education students, our ESE students, that spend a great deal of their time on a product called I Ready. And the company is very specific and very clear because this product is not to be used with children dyslexia. If we dive nose child in our county, is I Ready, who have dyslexia? It's not to be used with severely learning disabled students. This is our number one intensive instruction program for our struggling readers. And when you look at the research, is it research? Yes, it's research by people within the company, or people, a company that they pay to do the research and that it's not peer reviewed, it's not third party reviewed either. So one of the things that, again, it all comes back to that child's right to a free and appropriate public education. When that child has an IP, by law, the only instruction materials that the district's allowed to use to instruct that child, it has to be peer reviewed. It has to be third party reviewed. It cannot be a flash in the pan edtech product that is mastery based learning that a kid sits on a computer and just clicks through all day. There is no research that shows that that's appropriate for a child who has learning differences and unique needs in regard to processing, whether it be visual or auditory. And so, but we do know that teachers actually have the greatest impact on the educational outcomes of our students who struggle with learning disabilities. And there is reams of research that go back decades. And unfortunately, we spend a great deal of time taking these struggling learners and putting them in these intensive reading classes that are not something but computerized edtech software. But these children have to sit on every day, 45 minutes a day, sometimes 90 minutes a day, depending upon if there's a double block schedule. And it's not-- this is not what is-- it's just not OK. So my hope would be-- and every year, when this comes up for review and the district goes to purchase it again, I'm at the board meeting saying, I am asking you again. And I cite research. And I bring other studies. And I just say, please stop purchasing the stuff. And so I'm hoping that if I'm on the board, I can finally have a stay in the high quality instruction that we need to be providing our students, especially those with all the differences. So this is kind of my two big things for money. My priority

speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: Sure. It's very interesting because all of these answers are going to be so different than the last time we spoke because of the pandemic. This is bringing a whole new perspective to what is truly going to happen in the fall. Will we open school? Will we do a blended model? Will we stay closed and wait until spring semester to open? Nobody really knows. But one of the greatest things that happened due to this pandemic is the fact that this year we did not have any high stakes state testing, the FSA. Parents are thrilled. Students are relieved. Teachers are just thrilled, although kind of cautious because they don't know what accountability measure that the districts in the state will use when they go to either renew their contract or whether or not they get a raise or whether or not they're transferred to a different school. So that's a little nerve-wracking for teachers, but for families, we couldn't be happier. And when we look at the millions and millions of dollars that we spend on a single test, that it's ride or die with this test. I mean, you can't go to fourth grade. You are forcibly remediated in Vanity County based on that one test score. You are denied access to advanced classes, AP classes, some of the academically advanced students. You could have A's in all of your AP classes, and then you take the FSA and you don't get the three. And suddenly, you've lost some of your favorite electives, and you're now stuck in front of a computer every day during this mindless mastery-based software program, which is already very, very frustrating for families. So my hope is, and it's kind of looking like the disaster is going to actually make the call for us for next year. High-stakes testing will probably be eliminated again. So that's thrilling to me. So that would be something that I would-- if we do get back to school in the state, besides they want to try this again, there are options for families. It's called opting out.
